title: What Is Inflation?
paragraphs: Most people notice inflation long before they hear the word: the weekly shopping costs more, rents go up and the same salary seems to stretch less far. Economists define inflation as a sustained rise in the general level of prices, and because it affects everyone's purchasing power, it is among the most closely monitored indicators in any economy.

The key point is that inflation erodes the real value of money. If wages remain unchanged while prices climb, people can afford less, and savings held as cash gradually lose value. To measure the rate, national statistics offices use a consumer price index, tracking the cost of a representative basket of goods and services, from food and energy to housing and transport, and comparing it with the same month a year earlier.

Inflation can arise in different ways. Demand-pull inflation occurs when total spending outpaces what the economy is able to produce, allowing sellers to raise prices. Cost-push inflation, by contrast, starts on the supply side: when the cost of energy, raw materials or labour rises sharply, firms often pass the increase on to their customers. Rapid growth in the amount of money in circulation can add to both pressures.

Keeping inflation low and predictable is usually the job of a country's central bank, and many central banks target an annual rate of around two percent. Their principal instrument is the interest rate. Raising it makes borrowing more expensive and saving more attractive, which cools demand; the effect is not immediate, however, and typically takes months to feed through to prices.
